utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We are going to hear first from Dr. Nedopil, as I understand, if that's acceptable with you, Mr. Vujin? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One matter relates to a discussion we had about his appearance and that had to do with his fees. Mr. Vujin, you had indicated that his fee was about DM 1,000 an hour. I have been advised by the Registry that, in fact, it's DM 100 per hour. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I'm sorry, your Honour. There was a misunderstanding between my Belgrade-based office, which got in touch with Professor Nedopil, and the Professor probably spoke to them in English, which is not his mother tongue. That was probably the reason for this mistake. I imagine that now Professor Nedopil has accepted the Rules of the Tribunal, so I imagine it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No. I don't think an adjustment was made because of the Rules of the Tribunal. I think there was just a misunderstanding of what he would charge for his services for typically this type of service. Experts should be paid and it is quite appropriate. I just thought that it should be made clear for the record because it was important. It is not anything that we need to discuss when Dr. Nedopil comes, because experts get paid and they should get paid, but I just thought it was appropriate to discuss. One day I may want to be an expert witness and I would not want someone saying that I charged ten times the fee that, in fact, I charged. I don't think it's going to happen, but you never know. If there's nothing else, then let's bring -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): If necessary, I apologise to the court and Mr. Nedopil, but truly I had received a fax that that was the reason for this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I can understand that. Fine. Let's bring in Dr. Nedopil. (Witness enters court) (Interpreter enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Dr. Nedopil, would you please stand and take the oath that has been handed to you. Dr. Nedopil (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Vujin, you may proceed Examined by MR. Vujin MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Nedopil, would you please introduce yourself to this court with your full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): My name is Dr. Norbert Nedopil. I am from the Neurology Clinic. I work in Munich at the Psychiatric Clinic of the University of Munich in forensic psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Dr. Nedopil does not have earphones. There is an interpreter sitting next to him who, as I understand it, is interpreting simultaneously what is being said. I gather that Dr. Nedopil does not need any earphones; is that correct? Thank you. Mr. Vujin, you may proceed. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Professor Nedopil, how much experience have you had in forensic psychiatry? How long have you been working in this field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been working since 1982 as a forensic psychiatrist. Previously, from 1975 I worked as a clinical psychiatrist. Now each year I carry out about 40-60 evaluations. I'm in charge of the Department for Forensic Psychiatry at the University of Munich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Do you remember Mr. Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I September 1994 I observed him in the course of three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At whose request was this observation carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was at the request of the Federal Prosecutor of the Federal Court in Karlsruhe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this examination did you submit your findings in writing, as well as your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did write a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that report with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a copy of that report with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would request you kindly to read page 3 to us, which begins with the following words ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you want the doctor to read the entire page? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes. I want, because I have some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. You may read just that one page. I hope the 30 page report -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it really page 3 that you want me to read? Page 3, these are the charges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 4. Yes, that is precisely what I am interested in, the charges, so that I could put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, page 3 begins --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is in the German version, the interpreter might point out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This is a suspicion that the Serbs". In the English version this would be about halfway through page 2. (No translation). This is the bottom part of the first paragraph, which starts with: "As a member of the Serbian party and fanatical party of the Greater Serbian cause, the Serbs wanted to contribute to this ethnic cleansing".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is page 2, the first paragraph. The speaker was just continuing saying -- the speaker was continuing with the following, going on to page 2 of that version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Not meaning to interrupt, but I note on the English version, as we read this page, we are going to run into witness names, some of which were orders of the court earlier. As a measure we might have the doctor skip any names mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't see any names on the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you look towards the last paragraph of page 2 of the English translation, and the doctor is now about halfway down page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't recall that any of those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't recall that that particular witness was given protective measures. Both he and his wife testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. There is a name listed there, which wasn't subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Nedopil and Mr. Vujin, if that's acceptable to you, if it's not necessary for the names to be read out, then the doctor should not read out any of the names except, of course, for Mr. Tadic's. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): We would agree not to have the name of the protected witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you write the name down that you consider was protected and pass it to the usher? Judge Stephen would really prefer for it not to be read. I don't know how much you have read. If you want to put it into context, if for some reason you want this portion to be a part of the transcript, you tell me why, Mr. Vujin. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): We are only interested in this because of our further questions addressed to the Professor to see what his point of departure was. We want to see what his relationship was with Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. You may read it out, but Mr. Keegan is correct. There is -- the witness mentioned the third line from the bottom of the English version that is -- that was protected, and this report, was this placed under seal? This has been placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour but there are copies in Germany and my fear is by high-lighting a particular name you indicate who a witness is. I thought to avoid all names, then it avoids that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We heard two witnesses who were not protected but that's a common name. Doctor, you will read without mentioning any of the names in the report and it is very important that you do not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Mr. Tadic is specifically accused of the following: in the Omarska Concentration Camp the Serbs held approximately 3,500 Bosnian Muslim prisoners in the Summer of 1992 following a wave of ethnic cleansing. The inmates were kept by the Serbs in various warehouses, administration buildings, and garages in the former mining complex, depending on the estimated danger of their post. Interrogations, accompanied by grievous bodily maltreatment of the prisoners, were part of everyday life in the camp, as were systematic executions. In the so-called “red house” prisoners were tortured and then disappeared. According to statements from surviving camp inmates, they were killed like animals; for example, soaked in petrol and burnt alive. Prisoners had to load the corpses on to trucks for subsequent transportation. In the so-called “white house” torture preceded before the interrogations. Prisoners also died during this maltreatment". This is at the top of page 4 in the German version, in the middle of page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The next page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "As a Serbian militia man, the test subject had access to the concentration camp in Omarska, where he, as he had done many times previously, demonstrated his power and tyranny over the Muslim prisoners. On the 3rd June 1992 he, accompanied by three others, allegedly entered a room in which approximately 180 prisoners were packed together. The test subject and his three companions beat the inmates for two hours with rifle butts. One man was so badly injured by the thump that he received on the back of his head that he required medical attention. The test subject was allegedly the leader of the group. They did not leave the prisoners alone until they were tired of beating. On June 15th or 18th 1992 the test subject allegedly entered a garage, which was being used as a detention room, and demanded that the prisoners come out. After these prisoners had complied with this order, the test subject beat them with his rifle butt. When they were lying on the ground completely weakened he threw them one at a time into an inspection pit. Then he fetched the prisoner and ordered him to bite off the testicles of the three men. Some inmates in the detention room who observed the process heard the men screaming for two hours until they died. The acts were confirmed by five former prisoners, who were questioned by the Federal Criminal Police in relation to the conditions and events in the camp".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Nedopil. My next question is the following: before that, in your practice, did you have an opportunity to observe a test subject with such suspicions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to charges of this kind, no, I had not previously had perceived any evaluations in such a connection, but when it comes to comparably horrible crimes, I have indeed carried out evaluations on them. Usually, the victims of these horrible crimes were women and you can't proceed in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My question is the following. My next question is, are these things that the suspect, Dusko Tadic, then was charged with -- could this have influenced your objective opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I doubt that they would influence my objective opinion, because over the years I have become accustomed to dealing with a very great variety of people with various difficulties, and if you look at the end of my evaluation, you will see that when it comes to the judgement of the acts and the personality there, that I have taken it that what Mr. Tadic told me was true. That's one option I took into account. Then the other was that what the Federal Criminal Police office had said was true, that is to say that the charges were true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say that your findings and your opinion are objectively presented and in keeping with your professional knowledge and findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to me, Professor, what are the methods that you used when examining Mr. Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I talked with Mr. Tadic for several hours. I carried out various tests on him. I thoroughly considered his life history, his background, and I carried out physical and neurological tests, and with regard to the psychopathological considerations I asked him about all of those. Then my colleague, Dr. Werbauer, the forensic psychologist, carried out various psychological tests on Mr. Tadic, and these related in particular to intelligence, to any cerebral insufficiencies, personality, the profound psychological background, and then he considered the matter of simulation and dissimulation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all these tests acknowledged throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tests, as far as I know, are acknowledged world-wide. Now with regard to any difference of opinion, it's not on any national basis, but it's rather on the basis of schools of psychology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. These tests that guarantee at this level of the development of the science that you are involved in the possibility of truly viewing the personality of the test subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of the test procedures is 100 per cent foolproof. Now individual tests, in fact, may each have a broader spectrum of error, but considering different test results together, together with a psychiatric study, does provide you with a fairly accurate description of an individual and that won't reveal all the facets of an individual's personality, but that is not the purpose of the psychiatric evaluation either. There is always a specific issue that has to be addressed. So it's not a matter of considering each and every detail of the life and personality of the individual in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, having carried out all these tests, you managed to come to certain conclusions, so could you explain to us in the briefest possible terms what is the personality of Mr. Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to do so, as briefly as possible. Now, as far as the tests go, there's two things that emerged. Mr. Tadic was making an effort, in the course of the examination, as somebody who didn't attract attention. Looking at his life history and psychiatric evaluation you can see that this attempt to pass unnoticed can, in fact, be substantiated. We didn't find that there were factors that drew particular attention to that Mr. Tadic. Mr. Tadic is above average in intelligence and basically in the course of his youth he tended to be rather spoilt, and he could devote himself to his leisure and pleasures, and on the whole he seemed to be rather well integrated in his social environment. He is someone who likes to pass as balanced but is also someone who is seeking recognition, and you might even say that he tends to want to acquire a certain position, as it were, but this is not so pronounced that it would deviate from what one would expect, and, in fact, it is consistent with what you would find, shall we say, in the average person. Now, with regard to things deserving particular attention, we looked to see whether there were any sadistic tendencies that might be perceived and whether there were any tendencies to aggression that might be present, and on the basis of our evaluation we have to say that we did not see such tendencies in the course of the tests, some of which do bring out the presence of aggression without the test subject being aware of that, and even in these tests, as well as in the tests that are, shall we say, more straightforward, we did not detect any marked tendency to aggression. That said, there were some tendencies towards domination that emerged. In particular, as far as sadistic, sexual, etc., tendencies, we did not cover any tendencies of that ilk, so there were no marked characteristics that could be seen as motivating or providing an impulse for the charges that were alleged against Mr. Tadic at the time. Now he himself acted as someone who was balanced and who was always striving to steer clear of the opposing groups, and as a result of that lost a clear sense of self, and that's why he tended to join a group, and he did that rather reluctantly, and he also appeared as someone of a victim of unfortunate circumstances, which were due to the fact that precisely he didn't belong in any clear-cut manner to any one group or the other, and after his father died in 1990, he lost the support of his family, the support he'd enjoyed up to that point. Now, there was also a lack of self-assurance on account of the changes in social terms and economic terms, so that is what his case was until he moved to Germany. He did try on several occasions to move abroad, on one occasion to Libya and another to Switzerland. He tried to gain a foothold there, according to what he said, and he did not succeed, and that contributed to his social lack of self-assurance, as did the collapse of his small business that he had established. So to that extent, to the time of the evaluation, and in the previous period he was someone who was hurt in their self-confidence, but who tried to overcome that difficulty, and, for instance, in the course of the evaluation he emphasised the political role that he played. He said he had done a great job and even exaggerated a little bit in terms of being a middle man and helping in the build-up of his country. So if there were any shortcomings that might be touched on, on the one hand, there's lack of self-assurance, particularly in social terms and he tried to make up for this insecurity by exaggerating his political role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Did you establish that there were any psychopathological characteristics in Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Psychopathological, if you use that as meaning someone is suffering from a disease or something similar, if you take it as that, then I did not find any psychopathological characteristics, nor did I see any disturbances which would -- which might be referred to as pathological, just influences, etc. I don't think there were any of those present. I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to thank Professor Nedopil. The Defence has no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, your Honour. Cross-examination by MR. KEEGAN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Nedopil. I would take it then based on your conclusions, which you said were drawn from assuming certain factors, then you would say that Dusko Tadic has no psychological or pathological disease or defect which would provide an excuse or some mitigation for the crimes for which he has been convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I examined him from that angle, whether there might be any mitigating psychological disturbances, and I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you said at the beginning that your opinions and judgements are based on -- with respect to the evaluation are based on two factors. One is that you accepted what Dusko Tadic had told you as being true, and yet you also accepted that the acts for which he was charged by the German authorities were also true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first instance how did you reconcile then his absolute denial of any involvement or even presence in the camps with the fact that he was charged with crimes that occurred in those camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now the alternative that I indicated means that if what Mr. Tadic said is true, there's no need for any psychiatric evaluation, because then the matter of the question of being capable of feeling guilt or of assuming guilt for something one hasn't done, that becomes irrelevant. Now if, on the other hand, the charges are true, then there are no mitigating or quashing circumstances in the psychological sphere. So those are the alternatives that I reported to the authorities who commissioned the assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Dr. Nedopil, you are excused. You are free to leave. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness withdrew from court) (Interpreter withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, are you now going to continue with your submission as counsel as to the appropriate sentence, or have you completed it? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, your Honour, because our working hours were at an end, I was interrupted, and I am ready to continue today, but I would first like to inform the Trial Chamber that in connection with the request or suggestion that we prepare written evidence regarding the implementation of the law or rather the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia and connected with what I tried to explain to the Trial Chamber and which I should like to continue to explain in connection with Yugoslav legislation, we have prepared some of that material in the English language, and I will be glad to tender it, but that is a translation of the existing Penal Code of Yugoslavia, at least some Articles of that Code. Unfortunately we were not able to translate the relevant Articles of the Penal Code from 1997, which is in effect now. I have prepared copies in the Serbian language. I have contacted the Registry and asked them for permission to tender it in Serbian with the request that it be translated as expeditiously as possible, and this has been promised to us, so that you will have these documents for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, I have a question. You are providing the English translation of the existing Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are also providing in Serbo-Croat the Penal Code that was effective from -- from 1977 that is in effect now? If so, what are the differences between those two? I don't understand. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I am giving you in Serbian a copy of the law which was in effect up to the adoption of the new constitution and the new law of 1993, or, rather, I have to make myself clear: the criminal code in Yugoslavia was not changed. No new code has been passed. Throughout this period from the day it was passed until the present it was merely amended. This law exists since 1961 but it was amended in 1962, in 1977, and in 1993, when what is important for us, the death penalty was abolished. Therefore, we are only talking about amendments to that law, but the copies in Serbian are of the provisions that were in force at the time when the events in the municipality of Prijedor were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I should like to offer something I was referring to yesterday, and they are two judgements of the Supreme Court of Yugoslavia regarding the explanation that a crime against humanity can be committed only as a single extended criminal offence. I do indeed apologise that we did not manage to prepare a translation of this text. I was informed that the court has a translation and we were hoping that was the case, but anyway I hope that we will manage to have it translated, because it's not so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have been provided with a Prosecution submission, certainly portions of that, and if you can tell me what Article you are referring to. Is it chapter 16, Criminal Offences against Humanity and against International Law? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No. It's chapter -- no. What I have submitted to you in Serbian now is Chapter 1, the general provisions on criminal offences, the implementation of criminal law and the general institutes of criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does that begin: "Provisions of the general part of the Penal Code of Yugoslavia ...". No. That's the title of the annex. Does it begin with Article 19? There should be -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, it begins with Article 1, basic provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I see. I think we do have a translation. If we don't have a translation of all of the Articles, I think that we have a translation at least of some of them but we, of course, can have translations made. So let us see what the number -- Defence Exhibit 122 will be the Penal Code that was in effect from 1977 you have indicated until now. Excuse me. Then Defence Exhibit 121 is the English translation of the 1993 amendments to the Penal Code and then Defence 123 are two judgements in the Serbian language that you have referred to. Is there any objection to these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They will be admitted. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Your Honour, I should also like to submit to the court four additional exhibits tendered as evidence. One is Mr. Dusko Tadic's letter addressed to the Consular Offices of Yugoslavia in Munich on 6th March 1994 and we have had only a portion of it translated, which we feel may be of interest to you, and which indicates the readiness of Mr. Tadic to appear before this court. Actually in this letter Mr. Tadic insisted that the Yugoslav authorities intervene so that he may be brought before this court. Furthermore, three decisions in the so-called Ministers case from Nuremberg, January 1948; another one from February 1948, also from Nuremberg, and Vilezekta from Amsterdam, also from 1948, as judgements which may be of interest when thinking about the penalty that should be determined for Mr. Tadic. All these are in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, as far as I'm concerned, I think I have already certainly in the case -- in the Ministers' case read the judgement. What I would be assisted by on your behalf would be for you to tell me what portions of those three judgements you suggest are material and that we should look at. Can you do that? My recollection is that they are very lengthy, and I suspect that if we have no guidance from you, we may just look through them but be no better informed. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Honourable Judge, I have just prepared very brief excerpts which I feel you could focus on, but of course I am persuaded you wouldn't be a Judge in this Tribunal if you were not familiar with all the judgements passed in such cases and I had no intention of implying any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And you are going to tender the excerpts that you have in mind which you say are material. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes. Yes, the shorter -- the abridged version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In addition to discussing the nullem crimen issue that I referred to yesterday, I would appreciate if you would also address what effect the judgements regarding sentences in Nuremberg are relevant to this Trial Chamber's consideration. The Statute says recourse to Yugoslav sentencing practices, but just recourse. It doesn't say we are to limit ourselves, but I would like you to speak to the effect of the Nuremberg judgements particularly. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Your Honour, I am ready to comment on this, but I did say yesterday that I read and understand the Rules of this Tribunal in the sense that you are bound by the provisions of the Statute, and that in my opinion the provisions of Article 101 of the Statute are to some extent in contradiction with the provisions of Article 24 of the Statute and I will explain why. Article 24 of the Statute envisages as a punishment a prison term without elaborating on the duration of that period of imprisonment. Then the Article goes on to say that in determining the conditions for imposing a sentence, the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia would be taken into account. In my view, the mentioned provision can only be interpreted as implying that the length of imprisonment must be within the limits of the practice in Yugoslavia. I said yesterday, and I wish to underline today, practice cannot go outside the law, which would mean that to my understanding, and according to my interpretation of the Statute, the penalty that would be imposed according to the Rules of this Tribunal could not exceed a 15 year term of imprisonment as the maximum possible penalty. I'm saying this because at the time the Statute was passed we in Yugoslavia did not have life imprisonment as a possible penalty. I sincerely hope that no such penalty will be introduced into Yugoslavia, and it is quite evident that it will not. If as one of the conditions the Statute mentions practice in Yugoslavia, then that should have been accepted, or the Statute could have said that the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia will be borne in mind as well as similar cases as they were determined by the courts of other countries. As there is no such provision I see no connection with the Nuremberg processes nor the Tokyo trials nor any other trials, even the trials that I have now referred to and tender as evidence, that is the judgements that I have given, that could be of influence when considering the penalty for Dusko Tadic. Those judgements, in my opinion, could be relevant merely for reflecting initially on what are crimes, how they should be tried, what are the possibilities and so on, and I must point out in this connection that everything seems to indicate that unfortunately on this planet of ours there are many wars that are raging, and that only the events that happened in the former Yugoslavia are being tried. In this connection it is an essential need for a permanent international court to be established so that all those who do something that is unacceptable in such conflicts should be brought to justice. That is why regarding our position on the point of departure that you should adopt in our opinion, when considering the determination of the penalty with respect to Dusko Tadic, cannot under any circumstances be life imprisonment, as suggested by the Prosecution. In our view, in your deliberations, you must start from a maximum penalty of 15 years and after that taking into account the gravity of the offences of which you found Dusko Tadic guilty, the acts which you established beyond reasonable doubt as being committed by him, and linking this to the circumstances under which he did that, and I'm thinking of the overall madness, if I may describe it in that way, that swept our country, and linking this with the circumstances of the personality of Mr. Dusko Tadic, taking into consideration everything that was said in this courtroom, both by witnesses, Muslims and others, who spoke about his character, including today's witness, Professor Nedopil, through a system of elimination of all other facts which are not material for the determination of the penalty, that you reach a determination on a just penalty establishing the degree of criminal responsibility of Dusko Tadic as a man whose guilt you have established, whom you have to punish, but who was certainly at the tail end of events, as we say. So we are coming back to this question of big and small fish not in order to establish whether he was a person of importance, but I must assure you that apart from his relatives and friends, no-one had heard of Dusko Tadic before these events. I assure you that Mr. Dusko Tadic is far, far, far away from Karadzic regarding whom, when Mr. Niemann mentioned in his statement, I think he acted incorrectly. He has not been found guilty and he must be considered innocent until proven guilty, so that he could without reprimand in the way that I was reprimanded at one point, and I apologised, regarding my objections to Mr. Niemann's statements. I think it was incorrect to call Mr. Tadic Karadzic's henchman. I think the expression is inappropriate and that there is no reason to link the two together and this reference can be found in the transcript on page 209, line 15. Therefore Mr. Tadic was not a henchman, and particularly not did he work on anybody's behalf. Mr. Tadic was an ordinary man, an ordinary citizen who carried out some of the duties he accepted either under the work obligation that he managed to procure for himself instead of being mobilised to the armed forces, that is his duties as a reserve traffic policeman, or as an activist of the Red Cross and the local community, and for that reason and bearing in mind all his personal character traits that we have discussed here with the witnesses and that we have referred to, and indicating in particular his talent for art, and artists are surely not prone to the commission of any grave offences, I find that the circumstances which accompany the accused, Tadic, need necessarily be viewed in this light because Mr. Tadic was not praised or rewarded, because in those days only those were praised or rewarded who were successful on the front. I refer you to evidence, that is an excerpt from a daily paper, Kozarski Vjesnik, carrying a list of rewarded soldiers and only such people were rewarded for things that were happening there, no-one else, and therefore not Dusko Tadic either. Among those who were decorated were members of the military police, like Milo Dragavic, who were actually those who arrested Mr. Dusko Tadic. Therefore, viewing his personality in that sense, you will be in a position to weigh all that I have said and taking into consideration some further comments that I intend to make regarding Yugoslav law, I am certain that you will make a fair decision, which will not carry this or that message but only one message, that the international Tribunal -- that those appearing before the International Tribunal can expect only justice from that Tribunal. If I may now, I should like to try and explain some of my positions based on our criminal legislation, which we started to do yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We can read the legislation. As I indicated, when I said counsel's comments about it are perhaps helpful, but it's their view of the law and that's why we wanted the legislation itself. We can read that. I don't think it's necessary for you to read it and take us through that and then when you speak of practices and what is done, we need some documentation with respect to that. So if you have provided us with the statutes and you have provided us with decisions, we will read them. Believe me, we will. I think it's very evident what your position is. 15 years would be the maximum. We have no death penalty. We cannot apply the life sentence because it did not exist in the former Yugoslavia at the time and nullem crimen would be violated. I think you've made it very, very clear. I just have one question, and maybe I shouldn't ask the question. I thought I understood Professor Aleksic's testimony to be that the death penalty in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was abolished two years ago by the constitution. This is 1997, so two years ago would be 1995, but at least as far as the code is concerned, Serbia has the death penalty, Montenegro does not have the death penalty. If the death penalty was only abolished two years ago, and that would be in 1995, then in 1992, when these events were taking place, the death penalty was in existence and there was the option to sentence to 20 years if it was determined by the judge that the death penalty was inappropriate, but that the crime was so severe that it would be imposed instead of the death penalty, 20 years. Am I correct about his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you understood well on the basis of what was translated. Today, too, there were errors in the translation and a part of the statement of Professor Aleksic was misinterpreted. The part regarding the existence of the death penalty and 20 years as an alternative was translated well. However, when Professor Aleksic was speaking about the existence of the death penalty in Serbia and Montenegro a confusion occurred in the translation. I read through the transcript later. Namely Professor Aleksic did not say that there was no death penalty in Montenegro, but he said -- maybe the interpreter didn't hear well -- that Serbia and Montenegro for these offences do not have the death penalty because these offences are not regulated by the law of Serbia or Montenegro. These acts are covered by the law of Yugoslavia, these offences, that is by the Federal Penal Code in chapter 16. Therefore, I think that a small degree of confusion occurred, and that is why I wish to explain this by saying from 1961 our criminal legislation has been uninterrupted. We always had a Federal law in the former Yugoslavia which determined the general provisions, the general principles, and in the separate specific parts of the Federal law there were a series of criminal offences that applied to the Federation, including those against humanity and international law which were covered by chapter 16. In addition to the Federal Law, each republic, and until the amendment of the constitution also the autonomous provinces within the framework of Serbia, had their own laws, so that we had eight criminal codes in addition to the Federal one, which were more or less in accord and which covered what I would describe as ordinary crimes. Until 1973 -- I'm sorry -- 1993, when the last amendment was made to the Federal Law, in all our laws, that is in the Federal and in the republican, the death penalty was envisaged. However, in all our laws, and I have the text in English from 1961 with all the subsequent amendments, there is a provision which I sought to draw your attention to yesterday, and that is a provision that unfortunately you do not have in translation, a provision of Article 4 of the Federal Penal Code, which says: "The perpetrator of a criminal offence will be ruled according to the law that was in force at the time of the commission of the offence". That is paragraph 1 of Article 4. Paragraph 2 of Article 4 says: "If after the commission of the criminal offence the law is changed once or several times, the law that is more favourable for the perpetrator will be applied". We will have this text translated for you, so you will be able to read it. This provision, in my opinion, is very important, particularly because of the institution of nulla poena, because this obliges the Yugoslav courts to rule according to the mildest law from the moment of the commission of the act up to the trial. Therefore, if at the time the act was committed one law was enforced and after that another law was passed which was milder for the accused, and at the time of trial we have a third law, which is again more severe, the law which was in the meantime the mildest will be enforced. That provision on the application of the milder law gives us grounds to assert, as the Defence has already said -- of course it is up to you to accept this or not, but it is our firm opinion that you should accept this -- is that you cannot start out from a higher sentence than 15 years, because the death penalty has been deleted. This means that the alternative penalty of 20 years has been deleted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I see if I understand you correctly? In the first place you are saying that it is only the Federal Penal Code that we are concerned with if we are looking for Yugoslav law which deals with crimes against humanity, with war crimes, and therefore we need not concern ourselves at all with the penal codes of the republics. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Your Honour, if you rely upon crimes against humanity only from the domain of international law, then the answer is yes. Only the Federal Code regulates this subject matter. This is the case now and it was the case beforehand, and even before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And if we are looking at not merely crimes against humanity but war crimes generally, humanitarian law, the same objection applies, does it not? We look at the Federal Penal Code. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Only the Federal Penal Code is the code that regulates that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Right. There has been no relevant amendment to the Federal Penal Code dealing with those sort of crimes, which are called for convenience war crimes, in the last ten years; is that right? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But then you say that there is a further factor that arises, namely the abolition in some republics of the death penalty. Now what I don't follow is how that affects the Federal Penal Code to the extent to which the Federal Penal Code in relation to war crimes contemplates that the penalty may be death, and particularly if that abolition is an abolition republic by republic and not by the Federal Government, by the Federal legislation, by the Federal constitution, if you will. Do you follow me? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I have been trying to understand what you have been saying. I'm not sure that I have understood everything you said in its entirety, so, if necessary, we shall go back to certain things, but I shall try to explain. If you are only referring to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just before you do that, perhaps I can put it more concisely. We have got as the only relevant Statute the Federal Penal Code. However, that Federal Penal Code imposes possible sentences for what I've described as war crimes ranging from I think five years to death. What is the effect of the abolition in various republics of the death penalty upon the Federal Penal Code? That's all. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Your Honour, what republics? Could you kindly tell me that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it matters. Can the abolition by -- I don't know what -- the constitutional change perhaps, in particular republics of the death penalty can that have any effect on the effect of the Federal Penal Code? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I must answer that question by leaving aside what happened with the break-up of Yugoslavia, namely at the time of Yugoslavia's break-up, the secession of Slovenia and Croatian, and later Bosnia and Herzegovina too, at that point in time we had a single Federal Penal Code for all republics, that is to say the entire country, which prescribed the criminal offences of war crimes, and we agreed we would call them that for the sake of simplicity. That was the law which was amended in 1977 and which was in force at the time of the break-up of Yugoslavia and all those events. In that law at that time for those crimes the death penalty did exist, and it could have been replaced by a 20 year term of imprisonment from five years until the death penalty. At the same time there were penal codes in all the republics, but they do not regulate that subject matter and that is why we are not interested in that at all. After the break-up of Yugoslavia, Slovenia, Croatia, later Bosnia-Herzegovina, create states overnight, so they take over legislation. They take over the criminal code, the Penal Code of Yugoslavia as their own code, too, and immediately after that Slovenia and Croatia abolished the death penalty through the adoption of their new constitutions, and at that time in 1993 the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did the same thing, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia consisting of Serbia and Montenegro. Therefore, since we advocate the application of that code which was in force at the time when those events took place, the death penalty was applied then, but since it was changed, deleted through the amendment of the law in 1993, according to Article 4 we claim that not a single court of law can pass the death sentence for that crime, and therefore a term in prison of 20 years cannot be passed either, because that was there only as a replacement, as an alternative, and that is why we believe that 15 years is the maximum that can be imposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I then ask you one question? Assume that The Republic of Macedonia and it alone had repealed the death penalty. That would have no effect as far as we are concerned, Macedonia being entirely irrelevant to any charge which was laid against Mr. Tadic. What relevance has the repeal of the death penalty in the republics you have mentioned, which do not include Bosnia, to the situation as far as Mr. Tadic is concerned? You mentioned, you see, Slovenia, Croatia and Serbia. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Bosnia and Herzegovina. I mentioned later Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now I shall answer. Slovenia -- I'm sorry -- Bosnia and Herzegovina as a Federation now or rather a federation of entities -- I don't know what it is constitutionally speaking now; I couldn't explain that to you -- Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a new constitution. This new constitution, as we said yesterday, and I think that Mr. Keegan agrees with that -- with me on that, this new constitution took over all European and world conventions regarding this matter, since these conventions prohibit, and that is particularly the view of the European Community, they prohibit the death penalty, and Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted these conventions, but abolished the death penalty, too. With your permission, my opinion is the following. The existence of a law, which I'm not denying, in Bosnia-Herzegovina prescribing the death penalty for this crime, too, is no longer relevant to you because the law has to be in line with the constitution. This is a basic constitutional postulate of our constitutional law, that a law cannot be in contrast to the constitution, and, as Mr. Keegan explained yesterday, the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina is judging the constitutionality of that law, of that code, and therefore I believe that Bosnia-Herzegovina by adopting the new constitution also precluded the possibility of imposing a death sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have a further --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have a further question. Is there a particular section or clause of the constitution now in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina that you can point to which expressly abolishes the death penalty, or is it simply because there has been an adoption of various international agreements by Bosnia-Herzegovina and one provision of those agreements contemplates the non-enforcement of the death penalty that you say that is the result? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes, not prescribing it and that is what it says in the constitution. That's what we saw in the papers received from Mr. Keegan. What were the conventions that were taken over, and since these conventions were accepted, then it was also accepted that they could not prescribe the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What it says in the preamble to the constitution is that it is inspired by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and it goes on: "... economic and social and cultural rights and declaration of rights belonging to national or ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities as well as other human rights instruments". It is really wonderful, because the constitution has been inspired by these wonderful covenants. In the United States I suppose it may be inspired -- it does not say in its constitution -- inspired, but it has a reservation and routinely, at least in some states, enforces the death penalty. So what does inspire mean? What other guidance can we get from this constitution? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Every law has to be interpreted in the spirit of what the legislator wanted. If the legislator did not want to accept that, that they would abolish the death penalty, then the legislator would not have entered this provision in the constitution, mention of these international covenants, and the international covenant does make it obligatory for the signatories to that take-over, because the Penal Code also acted in accordance with that which is contained in the international covenants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujin. Are you complete with your submission? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No. In conclusion, in respect of the personality of Dusko Tadic, I would like to say a few more things. I believe that you have before you a person who, if we were to make a gradation of the possible degree of responsibility, he is at the lowest degree of responsibility. That is what you have to take into account when you pass the sentence. You have before you a person who is not different from other people. He was not a monster and you have before you a person who expects you to pass a just decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujin. The Prosecution, I know, has some things to say. I have some questions to ask the Prosecution as well. Particularly I am concerned -- we do need to recess but I am particularly concerned with the basis for the decision -- the statement that was made by Mr. Niemann yesterday, was it -- was it yesterday or the day before -- the day before that a sentence of life would really mean 15 years. What is your basis for that and we can talk about that after the lunch break. Also what effect does the principle of nullem crimen have on any sentence that we may impose in excess of 15 years? What is the relevance of the Nuremberg judgements? There may be more questions that arise but those are matters that we have talked about and we will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, or Mr. Keegan, whoever wishes to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, I will address some of the questions that have been raised by your Honours and Mr. Keegan will deal with some other matters very briefly. Your Honours, firstly, with respect to the 15 years in terms of sentencing a life sentence, which may amount to 15 years or less, I think probably it may be easier for me simply to hand to your Honours a table that we had prepared for this question, which does set out the position in a number of countries, including Italy and Norway, and if I can hand that up to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Finland, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finland, I should say, yes. Perhaps it doesn't include Finland. Yes, it does include Finland. When your Honours have that, I can just mention very quickly the law applicable to each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. I would ask that a copy be given to the Defence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Of course, before it's admitted, you'll need to explain how this was prepared and who prepared it, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I am not tendering it as anything other than an aide memoire for the court. If your Honours are not assisted by it, I will take it back. I only thought that it was rather nicely set out, the provision, but if there is any objection to it, I will simply withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now would you explain how this was prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was prepared by a survey of the relevant legislation of each of the countries that are there mentioned, looking at the issue of, question of parole, and it does address the question of remission on top of parole. It merely deals with parole. Then there is in some cases remission that is available on top of there, there being two issues there. Dealing, first, with Austria, Article 46, paragraph 5, states that: "Persons sentenced to life are eligible for conditional release after 15 years". In Belgium by law of May 31, 1988, Article 1: "A prisoner serving a life sentence can seek parole after ten years for one time offenders or 14 years for repeat offenders". I have no information on Bosnia-Herzegovina or on Croatia, or on Denmark. In Finland it is permissible for the court to sentence a person to imprisonment and can be fixed -- for a fixed period or for life, but there is no specific other provision relating to parole. In Germany, Article 453B of the Code of Penal Procedure deals with probation and supervision. Article 454 deals with conditional release and the Penal Code that indicates that a person sentenced to life can be released on parole after at least 15 years. I have nothing on Iran. In Italy the situation is slightly different. It provides that an offender -- this is Article 176 of the Code. Excuse me. 176 of the Liberadzoni Code. I think I have stated that correctly. It states an offender sentenced to life imprisonment can be admitted for additional freedom after having executed at least 26 years of the sentence. In addition to that, there is a provision which permits remissions to be earned at a rate of 45 days every six months of this sentence. That operates on the sentence. As I understand Italian law, and I don't profess to be an expert in any of these areas, that operates concurrent with this 26 year period. So if I can state it again. One earns remissions at this rate, the 45 days per every six months, but in any event one can be released after serving at least 26 years, depending on -- of the sentence. There is no similar such division in the Netherlands. In Norway according to the Prison Act any inmate who has been sentenced to imprisonment for more than 18 years may be released on parole when he has been in prison for at least 12 years. In Pakistan after 14 years imprisonment there is no right of imprisonment -- release, but the government can consider remission of the sentence. This is provided for by Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But the Prisons Act provides in Pakistan that a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment for life shall not be shortened to less than 15 years. In Spain prisoners who have observed good behaviour are eligible for conditional release on parole when they have served three-quarters of their sentence. The three-quarter requirement is mitigated if they have continuously participated in labour or cultural or prison activity, in such cases two-thirds of the sentence is sufficient to grant parole. I have no material on Sweden. In Switzerland Article 38 of the Swiss Penal Code provides that a person can apply for conditional release after having served at least 15 years of the life sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have been reminded, your Honour, in Finland the situation is that in respect of a fixed sentence, two-thirds of the -- after serving two-thirds of the sentence the prisoner can seek release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I don't understand the relevance of any of this. Let me put my difficulty to you. My understanding is that agreements have been entered into with two countries anyway for the imprisonment in those countries, Finland and Italy, of people sentenced to terms by this Tribunal, and each of those agreements says nothing at all about their own practice for remission or parole or whatever you like to describe it as, other than the fact that if local nationals become entitled to release after a certain period, then the matter is referred to the President for the time being of this Tribunal, and he makes a decision as to what to do. What is the relevance, other than perhaps a general survey to see what most nations tend to do with life sentences, to all this information, for instance, about Sweden and Spain and so on? Why does it help us in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I was attempting to respond to Judge McDonald's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How did you think you were responding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, my question really was, as I thought about it, the statement was made that, well, if he is sentenced to life, he will only serve 15 years. I asked what was the basis for it. Now you have given us this, but what Judge Stephen is referring to is something very different and that has to do with the agreements we have with the States and whether this really operates and that is: do the States control or does the Tribunal control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And do you have any submission on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ultimately, your Honours, the Tribunal controls in terms that the final decision has to be made by the President. It has to come back to the President. The point I was making is that there is certainly a grey area as to whether prisoners coming from this Tribunal would little (a) be eligible for parole or (b) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just a moment. When you talk about eligible for parole, I can understand that in relation to a national court and the prisoner remains in that country and is supervised, because that is what parole means. How do you conceive parole as operating in relation to somebody who is not a national of that country, and whom that country certainly does not want, I imagine, to be accepted as a new settler? What happens after he is released on parole? What possible application does parole have in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's conceivable in terms of supervision of the parole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is impossible, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the person stays in the country. That's unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How is he going to stay? He is going to be admitted as a new settler? That doesn't seem very likely, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Therefore can't we disregard this whole question of parole? Remission may be a different question altogether but it is not a question of parole surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, it may end up being that, but because it is discretionary in the hands of the President, it would be possible for the President to say: "The person has served this period of time and been of good behaviour during this period of imprisonment. Ordinarily the person will be under parole in the State and under supervision in parole" but that aspect of it could be waived. The President could say he could be released without supervision. It is entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So all this is relevant only to the guidance in years to come of the President for the time being of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me ask a question regarding the citation to the Finland law that provides that after two-thirds of the sentence an inmate may seek release, and if you can help me with Italy's law, if you can refer to a citation, if you know, as to when there would be an eligibility for release for fixed sentence -- fixed term of years. Actually, you know, Mr. Niemann, these are obviously problems, and counsel, that we are struggling with ourselves, trying to review the applicable legislation and then look at the Statute and then consider what type of control a Tribunal would have over a sentenced person, when perhaps the Tribunal will not be around in four years. So we would appreciate any assistance that either counsel can give to us, but I would also like you to give me some assistance on a citation to Italy or I can perhaps ask one of the legal assistants to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. If I can assist you, I would like to. The citation in Italy is -- the Italian Penal Code, title 2, Article 17, deals with the question of the life sentence and Article 176 deals with the question of the reduction of the sentence and conditional freedom after having executed at least 26 years of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's for life. I am really enquiring about fixed term, but if you cannot quickly locate it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not have anything for fixed term. That's all I had for life. My previous searches are only in relation to life, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, for a minute. Your Honour, we have the actual copy of the Italian code. It's in Italian and we will have to have it translated, but if we may, we could have it translated and provided to you, which I think might be easier. I am uncomfortable being so unfamiliar with Italian law to be making the submission on that say-so. I think I would feel better if I was to supply you with a copy of the Italian provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The same with Finland. We have several legal assistants who speak Italian, so they will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have the same in relation to Finland. If I may give an undertaking in relation to that. We will endeavour to do it as quickly as possible, but it will depend on the resources of the interpreters in terms of Finnish and Italian interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will resolve it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will certainly provide that to your Honours. Just to go back for a moment to what your Honour Judge Stephen was saying in relation to supervision, which is obviously going to be a very serious problem, I think, it was part of the reasons why, in my submission, I was saying that a sentence dealing with rehabilitation was -- that was primarily concerning itself with that issue was problematic, because there is a whole number of issues dealing with rehabilitation that couldn't be facilitated by this Tribunal, because neither is it, in my submission, reasonable for us to devise our own rehabilitative plan and programme for prisoners and then say to a State: "Follow this". I think that may present its problems. Secondly, and of course primarily, we don't have such a provision in place in any event, so there is nothing there for that to happen. It is perhaps in a confused sort of way my submission was to say in the absence of that aspect of rehabilitation and sentencing on the base of rehabilitation that is may be if remissions are earned for good behaviour and parole is granted for good behaviour, that may be in a sense a compromise to facilitate the element of rehabilitation which your Honours may be concerned about. It is possible, of course, not to deal with it at all; simply dismiss it as an issue and just deal with the question of punishment, but if your Honours were concerned about it, this seemed to me to be a sort of compromise position, but it doesn't go all the way in the sense that there's no supervision, and once the person is released on parole or after earning remissions, that's the end of the matter. That's about as far as I can take that, I think. Your Honours, dealing now with the question of nullem crimen and nulla poena sine lege, in our submission this has been incorporated in the international covenant for civil and political rights and in particular Article 15, and I hand up a copy of Article 15 and there is a copy for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 375, is that, subject to your verifying this chart for accuracy, do you have any objection to it? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): If the court is able to check the accuracy of this document we would have no objection to the document itself. We might have some other objections, but I would explain those later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It will be -- well, do you have objection to its admissibility at this time, or just the weight to be accorded it? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No. I don't understand really the effort of the Prosecutor to talk about remissions of penalty, and I have something to say regarding pardon or mitigation of sentence. We are now talking about the punishment and this is something quite different, if I understand it well. If this is related to the punishment, then would I be please allowed to express my opinion about it, because the Defence has not spoken about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution Exhibit 375 will be admitted. I imagine what you are saying is that punishment should be determined and the appropriate punishment. Now how much time, in fact, will be served, etc., is another concern that may not be relevant to the first issue, but subject to this being confirmed, it will be admitted, 375. Now 376 is a portion of Brownlie’s' basic documents. Any objection to this, Mr. Vujin? Page 282 and 283. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That will be admitted. You wanted to respond to 375.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your Honour, yes. I am not seeking to tender any of these into evidence. It is really part of my submission to assist the court, but I really don't -- I am not seriously trying to admit them as evidence in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't care how we proceeded. They have been given a number. They have been given a number. If you don't wish to admit them, Mr. Vujin would say don't give them to us. Attach them to your submission. What he wouldn't do is supplement them. I really don't care. Mr. Vujin, how would you like us to handle this? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): In my view Exhibit 375 should not be admitted as evidence, considering also the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: 375 is not admitted. It will be accepted as part of the written submissions of the Prosecution. 376.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Same position on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It will be accepted as part of the written submissions of the Prosecution. Okay. So neither of them are admitted into evidence. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. As I said, your Honours, Article 15 of the International Covenant deals with the principle of nullem crimen sine lege and nulla poena sine lege. It provides that no person shall be held guilty of a criminal offence. I am not going to read it all to you. The second sentence is the significant part with respect to penalty: " ... nor shall a heavier penalty be imposed than the one which was applicable at the time when the criminal offence was committed. If subsequent to the commission of the offence provision is made by law for the imposition of a lighter penalty, the offender shall benefit thereby". Your Honours, dealing firstly with this particular covenant, it, of course, is a covenant between States and doesn't purport to bind international organisations such as this, but I am not going to argue, your Honours, that your Honours shouldn't be at least -- comply with the provisions of it as such because it is an international instrument, and it's really more of a technicality that it doesn't apply to international organisations. The issue, though, your Honour, with respect to paragraph 1 of Article 15 is that it deals in a sense with the question of the application of a higher penalty than that provided for. In our submission, and Mr. Keegan will deal with this in greater depth, but in our submission if the penalty applicable at the time is the death penalty, then your Honours then don't have to concern yourself with this question of 20 years, 15 years, five years at all. What your Honours must be concerned not to do is to impose a penalty greater than the death penalty, which, of course, you can't do, I would submit, in any event. So assuming, for example, that the law provided that the maximum penalty was life imprisonment, and then assuming also that your Honours were not -- that the death penalty was available to your Honours, you couldn't then impose the death penalty above the sentence of life imprisonment. The life imprisonment would be the maximum penalty that you could impose. Then if there was sort of unusual provisions that operated below the life sentence and varied from State to State, in our submission your Honours do not need to be concerned about that in terms of the application of this principle. All your Honours need to be concerned about is not going greater than that which is provided for, but, as I say, Mr. Keegan will deal with that question. More significantly, in my submission, paragraph 2 of Article 15 is the important and operative provision. It says: "Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any persons for any act or omission which at the time when it was committed was criminal according to the general principles of law recognised by community of nations". In my submission this provision clearly on its face excludes the criminal provisions with which your Honours are dealing. Now there is some argument, I should say, to suggest that there is some doubt about how this operates in a national environment, because it deals with international laws in a national environment in Article 1, but at international law, in my submission, there is little or no doubt about the matter, that with respect to the question of penalties there seems -- it would seem that even as far back as the draft code in 1954 of the international law commission provided that the penalty for any offence defined in the code shall be determined by the Tribunal exercising jurisdiction over the individual accused, taking into account the gravity of the offence. The Article provides for the punishment of the offences defined in the code. Such provision is considered desirable in view of the generally accepted principle of nullem crimen nulla poena sine lege. However, it is not deemed practical to prescribe a different penalty for such offence. I will make -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Sorry. We have some problem with the translation. It's too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You didn't appear to be speaking too quickly, though.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was read out too quickly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will endeavour to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Rather than repeat the whole submission, I just emphasise, your Honours, at international law, as is reflected in the draft code of 1954 of the International Law Commission, in Article 5 -- it's now Article 3, I believe in the 1991 -- 1996 version of that draft the same provision is now provided which is the penalty for any offence defined in the code shall be defined by The Tribunal. Mr. Keegan will pick up on this point in terms of the Tribunal itself defining the penalty. Perhaps I might leave my submission at that point and I will make available to your Honours a copy of Article 3, which was previously Article 5. Unless there is any matters that help your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: This copy or these pages from Brownlie’s work set out the International Covenant that we were told and, in fact, saw has been adopted in the new constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the same covenant, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. On this issue of the principle of legality in the situation we are discussing I think we can summarise the principle of legality that is nullem crimen sine lege and nulla poena sine lege as the doctrine as providing protection that the crimes and more specifically for our issue the punishments which are applicable will not be created or imposed by this Tribunal to apply retroactively to an accused or punish a convicted person more severely than that person could have been punished at the time they committed their acts. They serve, if you will, to provide a protection against the abuse of power. Some of the argument we have heard flows from what could be called the strict positivist interpretation of those doctrines and they might argue that the Statute of the Tribunal is deficient in that it does not set out specifically the penalty for each of the crimes that fall under Articles 2 through 5. We believe when one looks at the application of the doctrine of legality in International Law and by States, particularly in the last half century, this strict interpretation is not borne out. Again we will cite to the ILC Draft Code. I think, to keep this presentation very direct, Article 24 provides a general framework for the penalties which are applicable in this Tribunal. Rule 101 then specifies the limit of the penalties and the circumstances that the Trial Chamber shall consider in arriving at a sentence. The authority of the judges to fashion Rule 101, of course, flows from Article 15. Thus, the Statute and the Rules meet the requirements of the principle of legality. Article 24 and Rule 101 are in consonance with the principles of legality because their terms are firmly rooted in terms of International Law and National Law which was in force in 1992 and they do not apply a sentence that is more severe than that which was applicable at the time that Dusko Tadic committed his crimes. The precedents found in both customary International Law and National Law which apply to such violations, that's violations of International Humanitarian Law support the imposition of a life sentence. In International Law we can look to such precedents as Nuremberg and Tokyo. In national law we believe you can look beyond the laws which applied in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia and can look to other nations which have tried similar matters, and that is these kinds of violations of international humanitarian law. So one could look to France, Australia, Canada, Israel, Germany, the other countries which have had war crimes trials, if you will. With regard to sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia, I do not wish to repeat our submissions regarding the decision in the Erdemovic case, except to say that is correct of course, the Trial Chamber is not bound by that or any other particular penal system. We can look to the fact that in 1992 such violations carried the death penalty. That would indicate that in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the law provided, as it did in most states at that time, for these kinds of violations the most serious punishment or penalty available under the law and we believe that is the relevant consideration here. Using that analogy then this Trial Chamber may say that the sentencing practice or Penal Code in effect in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time supports the imposition of the most severe punishment available to this Tribunal, and that is, of course, the life sentence. Now, with respect to Judge Stephen's question earlier about whether we are limited to the Federal code in the former Yugoslavia, we would submit that the court is not. We would submit that the language in Article 24 referring to courts of the former Yugoslavia envisaged a reference to both the republics as well as the Federal level in the former Yugoslavia, because, of course, at the time the crimes were committed by Dusko Tadic The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an independent state with its own Penal Code. The crimes were committed in the territory of that state and it would appear to us that it is the Penal Code of that state which would be the one you would look to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But it was the same as the Federal Code, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In this particular case it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So what does it matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
