utterances.text: Except if in 1992 there was a question about the application of the death penalty, for example, in what was then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that would not be the issue. It would be the question of was the death penalty applicable in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We believe that interpretation is valid when one considers the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. In other cases you will be having to look at the laws of Croatia which was an independent state at a certain period of time, perhaps even Slovenia should a case arise from there. It is not envisaged that you are limited to the old Federal law of the former Yugoslavia. With respect to Judge McDonald's question about the relevancy of the Nuremberg principles, we submit it would indeed be an odd interpretation of the principle of legality if it was well recognised, which we believe it is, that this Tribunal looks to the Nuremberg Charter and trials as well as to Tokyo trials for precedents and interpretation with regard to nullem crimen sine lege, half of the principle of legality, but then would not be able to look to those precedents for nulla poena sine lege, that's the penalty phase. In fact, we believe that this is borne out by the ILC in reference to the comments made by my colleague and I am citing now from UN document A/51/10, which is the report of the International Law Commission on the work of its 48th session, 6th May-26th July 1996. It is on page 29, which is commentary to Article 3, referred to by Mr. Niemann. Sub-paragraph 7. It is speaking about the application of the penalties. Article 3 does not itself describe the penalties. There was a debate between, in fact, if you will, 1954 and the present time about whether specific penalties should be addressed for each of the crimes. That debate has been resolved essentially back to the original language -- close to the language of the 1954 code and the Statute itself as it currently stands does not specifically set out a penalty. It references that an individual who is responsible for a crime against the peace and security of mankind shall be liable to punishment. The punishment shall be commensurate with the character and gravity of the crime. In the commentary, there, too, it says: If, on the other hand", referring to the penalty to be ascribed, "the jurisdiction lies with an international court, the applicable penalty shall be determined by an international convention, either in the Statute of the International Court, or in another instrument", presumably perhaps the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, "if the Statute of the International Court does not so provide". It is, in any event not necessary for an individual to know in advance the precise punishment, so long as the actions constitute a crime of extreme gravity for which there will be severe punishment. This is in accord with the precedent of punishment for a crime under customary International Law or general principles of law as recognised in the Nuremberg judgement and in Article 15 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. So again, your Honours, we would submit that the Statute and the Rules of this Tribunal are fully in accord with the principles of legality, and that the plain language meaning of Article 24, when it talks in terms of having recourse to this sentencing practice in the courts of the former Yugoslavia does not limit this court to those practices, or those punishments, and that this court can draw from that, as stated in the Erdemovic case, that in keeping with International Law these crimes, both in the former Yugoslavia and elsewhere, are those that merit the most severe punishment available to the jurisdiction. I have some information available on the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the applicability of the International Covenant, but more particularly the European Covenant, which is the covenant that is specifically referred to in Article 2 of that constitution as being applicable, and having priority over all other law in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So as to the question of the death penalty, I can only say that's on page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of that index we have gave you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Article 2, sub-paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You will see there it says: "The rights and freedoms set forth in the European Convention shall apply directly in Bosnia-Herzegovina and we shall have priority overall other law". Protocol 6 to the European Convention as a general matter abolishes the death penalty. However, in Article 2 it says that a State may make provision in its law for the death penalty in respect of acts committed in time of war or in imminent threat of war. So it in and of itself also allows for the death penalty for, if you will, war crimes, and presumably that would carry on for crimes against humanity and genocide committed during a time of armed conflict, which would mean for us Article 5 of our Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is the -- the suggestion is that the constitution, and I have them together -- constitution speaks of aspiring to certain rights, and I guess in the preamble -- then Article 2 incorporates certain rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are saying that notwithstanding the abolition of the death penalty as provided there in that convention, there is still left open to States who ratify or whatever is the procedure they use, to provide for the death penalty in war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: For war crimes cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Protocol 6 to the convention, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. What is the status of the Penal Code in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what are the provisions for ratification, or at least acceptance of the rights guaranteed by these conventions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At the current time the Penal Code in The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina still provides for the death penalty for a number of crimes, including Articles 142 -- 141 and 142, the sections which you have, which are war crimes, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The question that arises is two things. One, you have Article 2, sub-paragraph 2, which would seem to indicate that the death penalty will have to be abolished for everything but war crimes, but in addition to that, you then have this preamble language, which talks about the International Covenant and the universal declaration as well as others, and provides for later in the constitution a Human Rights Commission in Annex 6 and it talks about respect for the highest standards of human rights. Some would argue that would call for an abolition of the death penalty outright. My point the other day was there is certainly some ambiguity now as to what courts in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina could do at this time but as a matter of law the death penalty is still part of the Republic's law, and at least on its face would certainly apply for war crimes or the crimes which are subject in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As well as the 20 year option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And this -- the constitution came into force in 199 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: ... 5. After the Dayton agreements. This was, as you see, an annex to the Dayton accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is the relevant law? At what date do we look at the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We would submit, of course, that in terms of the question of the relevant law you would look to the law at the time the offences were committed. Certainly I think that with respect to a penalty one would have to say that under that sort of third aspect of nulla poena, if the death penalty has now been abolished, you could not now in turn impose it because it was in existence then. The question becomes: are you then also, if you will, left with only a 15 year maximum because you are stuck with, if you will, applying the laws that applied in the former Yugoslavia? That's when we say no, you're not. You have recourse to consider those but you are more specifically authorised as well to consider the precedents of International Law as recognised by the ILC and others and the Trial Chamber in the Erdemovic case, that the principle of legality is more than respected by the existing precedents available to you in International Law in terms of the rights of this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vujin, do you have anything to add to all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: To avoid repeating what I have already said, your Honour, I shall briefly comment on the position of the Prosecution that it is possible to apply the death penalty in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In our submission that is impossible for the reasons which we have given in our oral presentation. Also we still believe that there are contradictions between the provisions of Article 101 and Article 24 of the Statute of the Tribunal, because we feel the Rules have gone much further than envisaged by Article 24 of the Statute. We also still believe that you, as a Tribunal, in accordance with the provisions of the Statute are bound to take into consideration only the practice in the former Yugoslavia, because that is how that rule should be understood, otherwise the Statute would have said "the practice in other countries or in similar such cases". What I would like to say in answer to the comment by my learned friend the Prosecutor, they are subscribing to the application of the heaviest penalty for such cases without trying to individualise the penalty, to establish the circumstances under which this concrete accused committed an offence, and to take into account the circumstances of his personality, which I'm sure you will take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Vujin -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): In my view, you can use the maximum penalty only as the starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't think that we need to re-hear everything that Mr. Livingston said about individual circumstances, Mr. Kostic and you yesterday also. I wish you just to respond to this question of law. Otherwise we will go back and forth forever. I understand individual circumstances. Just as to the law, if we can. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Will you please then address the question to me? I do not understand what I'm being asked. I have answered all questions so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you have any comment. I don't think you have. I think we have gone back and forth enough on it. You have told us what the law is in the Federal --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I just said that I abide by all that I have said and I just repeated that the positions of the Prosecution were unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You have told us the law in the former -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Professor told us the incidents occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have talked about recourse to the laws of the former Yugoslavia. I gather it's your position that we shouldn't even look to Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it's just the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that we should look to? Is that your position as to the law? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No, I never said that is correct your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): I always use the term "the former Yugoslavia" and Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia have the same law as the one that was effective in the former Yugoslavia. That is the point. Their laws contain a provision that is contained in Article 4 of the Federal law. I do not have their laws at this moment, but we will submit them in writing. This provision from Article 4 from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is that necessarily the lighter penalty has to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's what the international -- MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That has been drummed into us. We understand that. Bosnia-Herzegovina has not abolished the death penalty by code. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has. Slovenia has, Croatia has. So there are different implications for that and we understand all of that. I just want you to make sure you are aware that we are looking at all of the republics of what were the former -- what was the former Yugoslavia. MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): That is our position, too, because only in that way will you be able to apply the law properly, but I just wish to comment on what the Prosecution has said referring to a draft of the International Law Commission. I think that was the draft of the Statute of a permanent criminal tribunal. I would like to say that you are not bound by those positions, because if that Law Commission could have resolved all the problems, we would have had a permanent international tribunal rather than the international community forming this Tribunal to try crimes committed in only one part of the planet. That is one point. Second, the Erdemovic case also cannot be taken as being material for your decision-making. It can serve as a basis for authority in view of the consequences that Erdemovic produced as opposed to the consequences of the acts that you found Dusko Tadic guilty of, but that is not binding for anyone in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have anything else to offer on behalf of the defence? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Yes. We have our concluding position, that with respect to the penalty that you have to pronounce our position is, as Dr. Kostic said yesterday, that the time spent in detention so far is an adequate punishment for the offences you have found him guilty of, and that that should be your sentence and he should be immediately released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Niemann, or Mr. Vujin, that you wish to offer? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): Mr. Tadic would like to make a statement at the end, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Tadic -- I think the lawyers are conferring. Mr. Tadic, if you wish to say anything at this time, you may be afforded the right to. You are not required to, of course, but if you wish to say anything on your behalf, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TADIC
utterances.text: I thank you for this opportunity to say something, and if I may be allowed by the Trial Chamber, I should like to read a note that I took down in the break. I do not feel capable of speaking by heart. Honourable court, I sincerely regret that the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am sorry for the suffering of the civilian population in the Municipality of Prijedor and especially in Kozarac. As a citizen of the Republika Srpska and a resident of the Municipality of Prijedor I had to behave in accord with the civilian and military laws on mobilisation which were in effect in the territory of the Republika Srpska in 1992. By decision of the Crisis Staff -- the decisions of the Crisis Staff were law, and any refusal was treated as desertion. I never attended any military exercises. I did everything to avoid being mobilised into the army of Republika Srpska in 1992/1993. Members of traffic policemen were never wartime units before, during nor after the war operations in the Municipality of Prijedor in 1992. I was not a soldier from 1991, like Goran Borovnica. I was not the Prime Minister of Kozarac, as Branko. I was not President of the local community like Bosko Dragicevic. There never was a local board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was not President of the Serbian Democratic Party, like Simo Miskovic. I was not a military officer, like Major Zoran Karlica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Slow down just a little bit, because the interpreters are trying to translate, and you have probably seen, Mr. Tadic, we have had that problem throughout the trial. Slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TADIC
utterances.text: I was not Commander of the Serbian Army of the Municipality of Prijedor, like Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja, on the basis of whose name in 1992 after the war operations in Kozarac my native town was called after him Radmilovo. I was not a Commander of the Municipal Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality, like Dr. Milomir Stakic, who is today President of the Municipality of Prijedor. I was not a guard in any camp in the Municipality of Prijedor, like Mladen Radic and others. I was not a commander of a single camp, like active policeman Zjelko Meakic and Professor Slobodan Kuruzovic. From June 16th, 1992, I was a reserve traffic policeman on duty checking the security of passenger and freight traffic -- civilian traffic. I was not the Head of the patrol of traffic policemen, like Miroslav Brdar. I was not commander of the traffic police of the Municipality of Prijedor, like Dure Prpos. I was not Commander of the General Police, like Dule Jankovic. I was not Chief of Police of the Municipality of Prijedor, like the lawyer Simo Drljaca. I never had any military rank, nor was I ever decorated or praised by the Military Police or civilian authorities of the Municipality of Prijedor. I was not a soldier like Dule Knezevic, with special merits. I was never praised by the Commander of the Army, by Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja. Those who were praised were members of the Military Police, including military policemen Vijic, Milo Dragovic, who arrested people and mobilised them into Republika Srpska. I am not Mico Danicic, because he was rewarded for the acts of which I have been found guilty. I was never a councillor of the President of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic, who, as a reward for the acts of which I have been found guilty, has his own councillor, Mico Danicic. I co-operated with this court from the day of my arrest in February 1994 in Germany to the present. I made statements over 50 hours to investigating bodies. I asked to be tried by this International Tribunal in The Hague, believing in its fairness and justice. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. You may be seated. Is there anything else, Mr. Vujin? MR. VUJIN (in interpretation): No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? The sentencing is scheduled for July 14th at 10.00 am. We will stand adjourned. (3.30 pm)
